content: The guidelines are grounded in a public health approach, aiming to address the health needs of populations by ensuring broad access to essential services and medications. The Guideline Group emphasized that this strategy is most effective in promoting equitable access to affordable medicines. Regarding patient preferences for insulin types in type 1 diabetes management, a narrative review presented to the Guideline Group revealed that long-acting analogue insulin was associated with significantly higher patient satisfaction compared to intermediate-acting human insulin in four studies. Among eight studies comparing short-acting analogue insulin with short-acting human insulin, two studies (including the only blinded study) found no difference in satisfaction, while six studies reported significantly higher satisfaction with short-acting analogue insulin. For studies comparing biphasic insulin or basal-bolus regimens, one study indicated a preference for analogue insulin, while another found no difference between groups. Factors influencing treatment satisfaction included flexibility in treatment or diet, convenience, reduced perceived hyperglycemia or hypoglycemia, improved blood glucose stability, and reduced fatigue. However, the Guideline Group noted that most studies had a high risk of bias, and in the single blinded study, patients could not distinguish the type of insulin they received. This made it challenging to fully account for patient preferences and acceptability of different insulin types. The feasibility of applying findings from clinical trials conducted in high-income countries to routine healthcare in middleand low-income settings was a concern for the Guideline Group, especially given the rising prevalence of diabetes in these regions. The recommendations were based on available evidence, with concerns addressed in the research gaps section of the guidelines. Several research gaps were identified during the evidence review and recommendation development. Operational research is needed to evaluate treatment effectiveness under routine conditions in low-income countries, as opposed to controlled trial environments. Studies exploring barriers to care access and context-specific interventions to improve patient adherence are also required. For oral hypoglycemic agents, trials of new medications should include metformin and sulfonylurea as comparators rather than placebo, particularly for long-term outcomes where data is limited. Questions remain about treatment options and medication combinations for type 2 diabetes, such as whether adding a third oral agent delays the need for insulin and the role of combining new oral agents with insulin. Continuous monitoring of side effects for newer medications is also necessary. Epidemiological research is needed to better understand the burden of diabetes, particularly type 1 diabetes, in low-income countries. Current estimates of the number of children and adults with type 1 diabetes in many countries are likely inaccurate, complicating insulin procurement due to uncertainties about the population in need. The guidelines will be available for download on the WHO website, and the systematic reviews and evidence used in their development will be published in peer-reviewed journals or made available online. WHO regional and country offices will encourage implementation at the national level through their contacts with ministries of health, providing technical assistance if substantial country adaptation is required. The updated recommendations will be part of the technical package of the WHO Global Hearts Initiative, which builds on the WHO PEN initiative to improve cardiovascular disease prevention in primary healthcare. WHO will monitor the adoption and implementation of the guidelines in national policies and programs by reviewing the number of countries that have adapted or endorsed the guidelines. The Global Hearts technical package, currently under development, will include clinical and process indicators for diabetes, using routinely collected data from service delivery forms, registers, and monthly summaries. The toolkit will be piloted in Barbados, Colombia, Ethiopia, Nepal, the Philippines, Tajikistan, and Uganda. The guidelines are expected to remain valid for five years, reflecting the likelihood of new research findings during this period and the feasibility of updating the guidelines considering costs, time, and resources. If significant changes in evidence or user needs occur before the five-year mark, updates may be considered sooner. Clinical trials comparing sulfonylurea and metformin with newer agents in their effects on cardiovascular mortality and complications of the kidneys and eyes would be particularly relevant for future updates. However, such trials, especially those independent of industry funding, are rare and require more time than those focused on surrogate outcomes like glycemic control. The existing evidence on glycemic control and hypoglycemia is relatively robust and unlikely to change significantly with new trial data.
